subtopic: PROPOSAL TO AVOID REDUCTION IN PRODUCTION OF HEAVY OIL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
PROPOSAL TO AVOID REDUCTION IN PRODUCTION OF HEAVY OIL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the terms of Standing Order 43. I am compelled to do this by the extremely grave threat to Canada's heavy oil production caused in part by the export quota system which has lead to a dramatic fall in demand. Already over 500 of the Lloydminster producing wells have been shut down and due to the unique characteristics of the Lloyminster field, these wells may never again attain full production when restarted. I therefore, move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin):
That although this House acknowledges the efforts of the National Energy Board to deal with the situation, this House regrets that the measures will not become effective until March or April, 1976, thus forcing the closure of many more oil wells in the Lloydminster area causing severe disruption of the economy and the subsequent loss to Canada of vital oil resources, and directs the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to make new initiatives, possibly entailing either the further reduction of the export tax on heavy oil or the exemption of heavy oil from the quota system.

speechtext:

speechtext: Arising out of the statement in the House on January 9, 1974 by the then minister of energy, mines and resources that with regard to Venezuela we were making clear Canada's interest in the continued assurance of supply from that country and the possibility of an accord, et cetera, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he discussed this long term accord with respect to the security of supply of oil from Venezuela during his visit.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: VENEZUELA-DISCUSSION DURING PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT CONCERNING PURCHASE OF OIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, only in the sense that I indicated in my answer, I believe to the Leader of the New Democratic Party, yesterday. There was no precise accord exchange of quantities or figures. As I think I indicated yesterday the Venezuelans now are interested in an assurance that we would not lower the general magnitude of our liftings because of the nationalization that they proceeded with, and I could give them that assurance. On our side, we were interested in making sure that they were going to consider Canada as a market to which they would be continuing to export without any political conditions put on their exports. subsubtopic: VENEZUELA-DISCUSSION DURING PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT CONCERNING PURCHASE OF OIL
speechtext: That particular Latin connection seems to be a little loose. May I take it, then, that the Government of Canada is no longer pursuing the policy outlined by the then minister of energy, mines and resources? subsubtopic: VENEZUELA-DISCUSSION DURING PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT CONCERNING PURCHASE OF OIL
speechtext: If I can use an appropriate metaphor, the shoe is on the other foot. Venezuela at this time is interested in making sure that Canada takes all the oil it wants to export, and therefore the kind of preoccupation suggested by the Leader of the Opposition is not at all appropriate.

subsubtopic: VENEZUELA-DISCUSSION DURING PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT CONCERNING PURCHASE OF OIL
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: VENEZUELA-DISCUSSION DURING PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT CONCERNING PURCHASE OF OIL
speechtext:
I am referring to a preoccupation of the government which existed back in 1974, and in view of the

fact that an increase in percentage of crude petroleum coming into eastern Canada, upon which eastern Canada is dependent, is now coming from parts of the world which can hardly be considered stable, I ask the Prime Minister whether it is the view of the government that the shoe is really on the other foot; that it is up to Venezuela to worry about selling oil to Canada; that Canada, particularly eastern Canada, can feel quite secure about the supply of oil and that the worries the then minister of energy, mines and resources had following the crisis or the near crisis of a year or two ago have been completely forgotten by the present Prime Minister and the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.

subsubtopic: VENEZUELA-DISCUSSION DURING PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT CONCERNING PURCHASE OF OIL
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, that has not been forgotten, but I am sure the Leader of the Opposition is in a position to realize that questions of supply sometimes predominate and questions of demand sometimes predominate. At the present time Venezuela is more concerned with demand for their oil than we happen to be about supply. That does not mean that at a different time in world events the situation will not be different and the shoe will not be on the other foot. That is why, in general, it was very important to make sure that our relations at the political and commercial level with Venezuela remain very good. At this time they are, in a sense, perhaps asking us for something of a favour but a couple of years ago we were asking them for a favour. This is the meaning of the Latin connection, Mr. Speaker, that we help each other and this is the kind of relationship we have established with Venezuela.

subsubtopic: VENEZUELA-DISCUSSION DURING PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT CONCERNING PURCHASE OF OIL
speechtext: One final supplementary, Mr. Speaker. In view of the importance of even this government looking more than a year or two ahead and if the Prime Minister found that the government of Venezuela was anxious to encourage sales to Canada, would this not have been an excellent time for the government of Canada to have achieved an increase in the security of supply of oil for the Atlantic provinces, Quebec and the eastern part of Canada?

subsubtopic: VENEZUELA-DISCUSSION DURING PRIME MINISTER'S VISIT CONCERNING PURCHASE OF OIL
speechtext:
Well, it would, Mr. Speaker; in the very general sense I have admitted it would. The Leader of the Opposition will, of course, realize that the kind of question asked by the Leader of the New Democratic Party is also relevant, here, however. We want to make sure that, given the particular quality of that particular source of oil, we will be paying the right price and there was no need at this time to embark on any specific bargain. Of course, I repeat, that Petro-Canada is going to be sending a delegation there to examine this question and perhaps to embark upon some bargaining. I must remind the Leader of the Opposition, however, that in Venezuelan terms they do not have an eternal supply of conventional oil. They are thinking in terms of ten or perhaps 15 years and they are asking us for support in the exploitation of the Orinoco tar sands; they are talking exchange of technology with us.
In these various senses our relations are good and will continue to intensify, but we should not think that a guarantee against all future eventualities. Venezuela has a secure supply of oil. The time is limited, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the question period I was allowed to put a serious question to the Minister of National Defence. That question dealt with an urgent situation that occurred at the beginning of the week, namely on February 2, in Quebec, and more particularly in the areas of Montreal, Saint-Hyacinthe, Drummond and Quebec City.
Indeed, during that violent storm thousands of families had to do without essential services like electricity, heating, water supply and so on. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, hundreds of car drivers were also trapped on Highway 20 and regional roads. This put the lives of thousands of people in danger.
I personally witnessed that hundreds of other people stuck for hours were able to hear on station CKVL calls of distress from mothers of families who were asking for help to have either heating or water to give to their children. At that time, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian army was also being called upon because, finally, all Canadians pay to maintain thousands of people who must safeguard the rights of Canadians and come to their help in difficult times.
Well, I asked myself how it was that the Canadian army could not come in to rescue those people whose lives were in danger. That is, Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege.
Earlier I wanted through Your Honour to ask the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) what were his

powers when such situations occur and which allow the Canadian army to come to the rescue of people or families caught in excessively difficult situations.
Some of my colleagues on the government side seemed to find the intervention by the hon. member for Bellechasse funny.
Mr. Speaker, this is no joke but a tragic situation, and God save those people from needing help from people, or even the Canadian army. It is necessary to live excessively difficult times and even see one's life endangered to understand all the grandeur of the life God gave us. And when it is put in danger because of events or exceptional circumstances one must seek by all means to rescue one's neighbours to protect and safeguard them.
Mr. Speaker, last week I asked the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) who is now in the House, a very serious question. I asked him whether he had received a request from the Quebec government and the City of Montreal that members of Canadian forces be posted in Montreal during the Olympic Games. The minister earnestly replied that he had. In a supplementary question, I asked him what would be the cost of the Canadian army's participation in the games; he answered, as reported on page 10430 of Hansard that this participation would cost about $24 million.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the minister for this information. If it is deemed desirable that Canadian forces be present at the Olympic Games, I wonder, on behalf of my fellow Canadians, whether when difficult situations arise, as was the case early this week in the areas I have mentioned earlier, we should not be entitled to expect that Canadian forces which are well equipped with trucks, ploughs, blowers and snowmobiles, provide Hydro-Quebec staff with assistance?

speechtext:
As is sometimes said, it might not be necessary to hear further discussion. I do not want to restrict hon. members who wish to intervene in support of the hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Blais). I want to make that clear. We could take it as a general indication that if any hon. member seeks the floor in support of the hon. parliamentary secretary's argument, I shall hear from them now. On the other hand, if their intention is to support the procedural regularity of the motions put forward, I do not think it is necessary to hear them.
My view is that the bill is a bill to amend the Income Tax Act. Pursuant to the Income Tax Act as it now stands, without passage of Bill C-58 it is possible for taxpayers to advertise in foreign broadcasting undertakings and deduct those expenses from their income. The purport of Bill C-58 would be to change that and take away from those advertisers the opportunity to make those deductions from income. Whether it be that clause 3 contains an actual provision or not, the fact of the matter is the amendments put forward by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) would in fact propose what seems to me to be middle ground, that is, advertisers who advertise in foreign broadcasting undertakings would be permitted to deduct from income the expenses paid for those advertisements, provided certain conditions are met. The conditions are complex and will need some explanation, but that bears on substance and their acceptability to the House by way of a vote. It does not bear, in any way that I can see, on procedural regularity.
It seems to me that the hon. member ought to be able to put that kind of motion by way of amendment to this particular clause. It would be my view that motions ought

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a brief point with respect to the speech made last night by the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) questioning, not the substance of the bill but the propriety of the minister in seeking to interpret the words in the statute. The hon. gentleman delivered a scathing denunciation of this practice. I might even describe his language as brutally frank. He found the situation "shocking"; he found it a "complete usurpation"; he found it "completely revolting"; he was "filled with distaste"; he found it a "complete subversion of the judicial process", and thought it "entirely arbitrary". These are strong words, Mr. Speaker. The hon. gentleman whipped himself into a veritable lather of indignation about this supposed transgression on the part of the minister.
As a relative newcomer I am, frankly, surprised to find the hon. Leader of the Opposition make this statement in regard to the role of the Department of National Revenue

in giving an interpretation of the Income Tax Act. Surely he is aware that the department is called upon constantly to give such interpretations. Since 1970 the department has published over 280 interpretation bulletins performing just this function, informing the taxpayer how the department interprets the law. The public expects this service and constantly requests the department to increase this flow of information. As well, the department issues rulings to specific taxpayers on specific situations advising them how the department will assess.
I will not take much more of the time of the House. I repeat: the interpretation made by the minister is the same as the interpretation made by his officials on their reading of the law. If a taxpayer wishes to challenge that interpretation, he may take the matter to court and have the court interpret it.

If in the normal course of appeal the courts disagree with the interpretation of the department, the government will, as it has in the past, bring vew legislation before the House by way of a motion of ways and means to correct the error. I suggest that is how the system has always worked and that is how it will work now. There is nothing new about it.

That ruling, or interpretation, was challenged successfully in the courts and in November, 1974, the budget was debated and passed in parliament and legislation was enacted to support the original interpretation.
Clearly, this is no subversion of the system, as the Leader of the Opposition suggested. I suggest that the tongue-lashing he gave the government was inappropriate and unworthy of his usual wisdom in such matters.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am amazed at the moderation shown by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). When I consider the words he could have used, I am amazed by the words he did use. Only because he is such a mild and reasonable man did he restrain himself to such an extent yesterday and use that kind of language. Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Mississauga (Mr. Abbott) I, too, was going to refer to the words used in the speech last night by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), but I intended to put a different connotation on them. When the Leader of the Opposition described the government's latest move on Bill C-58 as completely shocking, revolting, a subversion of our whole judicial system and acting in an arbitrary way, I intended to suggest that his language was not strong enough. The government is really undermining its whole position on this bill.
Certain facts have to be brought out in order to inform the Canadian people of precisely what is going on. I think the first response one must make, in commenting on the remarkable speech and tortured explanation of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) regarding the move to allow Reader's Digest to come under Bill C-58, is to say that this is a prime example of why the government should not be involved at all in the interpretation of what publishing is in Canada. The minister has done a disservice to that element of fairness which the government said was in its mind in bringing forward Bill C-58.
Yesterday, the government announced that Reader's Digest would suddenly qualify under Bill C-58, without ever hinting during all the committee hearings that they felt Reader's Digest would in any way qualify. What the government has done is completely reverse its decision. I submit that the Canadian people will not accept that kind of arbitrary change as being fair, particularly when it has no basis in law.
We on this side of the House are in a difficult position. Many members of the Conservative party argued that the application of Bill C-58 would be unfair to both Time and Reader's Digest and considerable effort was made to get the government to change its mind, particularly in the case of Reader's Digest. We now have a situation in which Reader's Digest is going to qualify for continued publication, with its advertisements being exempt for tax purposes. That is what we wanted. What we did not want was this decision brought in through a back door deal in a way unfair to the members of this House and to the whole publishing industry in Canada.
The committee held a number of hearings on this bill and a great amount of debate took place on second reading. During all that time the government gave no indication of a change of heart, and has now suddenly reversed itself without any basis for such a reversal. The opposition to this kind of decision by fiat should be continued in order that the government will know this kind of conduct is not

February 4, 1976

acceptable to members of this House and is not an answer to the publishing problems in Canada which the bill set out to correct.
The editors and publishers of Time magazine are entirely within their right to speak as the president of Time Canada did last night when commenting on the new arrangement between Reader's Digest and the government, an arrangement that was sprung on everybody. I think Mr. Stephen LaRue was within his rights when he said there is no doubt that there was a bit of secrecy involved in these negotiations. Mr. LaRue went on to state:
It certainly raises some questions about last-minute deals. The public needs a clarification now of what the agreement means.
We are now in a remarkable situation. Reader's Digest will not have to change anything it is doing now regarding the manner of its publication. It will be able to go ahead and continue to publish and meet the demands of Bill C-58. Representatives of Time magazine came before the committee and told us about a proposed plan whereby it would make changes in such a way that half the publication would be of fresh material originating in Canada, and half would be imported from the United States parent, but that the entire package would be edited in Canada. That was a substantial move by Time, in the interests of complying with the intention of Bill C-58. Time came before the committee to say it would change to accommodate Bill C-58, but Time has now been rebuffed.
It was well known that the intent of Bill C-58 was to stop the special status that both Time and Reader's Digest have been enjoying since 1965. What we have now is a reversal of that intention. We will still have a special status for Reader's Digest. However much those of us who wanted Reader's Digest to continue publishing in Canada, as it now does, are in favour of this move, we certainly oppose this kind of decision-making process which in our opinion is completely unfair and without foundation in law.
Time magazine is entirely correct in posing a question to the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) in an article which appeared in the February 9 edition in answer to a letter it received from the minister. In this article, Time sets out its opposition and objection to the content rule by stating:
It has no mooring in the law as parliament approved it in 1965. To say that "not substantially the same" means "more than 80 per cent different" not only distorts the law but violates the English language.
The amendment we are debating now, to which the Minister of National Revenue addressed his comments last night, has to do with content-and content is the heart of the bill. We ought to bring back into focus what we are trying to do in this bill in respect of publishing. We want to help Canadian publications. Representatives of Canadian publications and their advertisers appeared before the committee and were entirely divided on whether the bill would be of help to them. What everybody agreed to was that the provisions of Bill C-58 would be all right if they confined the requirement to 75 per cent ownership in Canada without a content rule. It is the insistence of the government on this extreme 80 per cent content rule which is at the centre of this controversy.
We now have this apparent violation of parliament's right to make sure that the legislation we pass in this House is fair to all concerned. The thrust of the objection

this afternoon is related to the arbitrary decision by the government that a group of officials in the Department of Revenue should be empowered to decide what is "substantially different" under the 80 per cent formula and therefore able to qualify. We object to this arbitrary decisionmaking which exempts Reader's Digest under a new clause that is unfair and without foundation in law.
I think it is interesting, as we continue to focus on the heart of this issue, to look at the comment which was made by Geoffrey Stevens in the Globe and Mail. Greater attention should have been given to this aspect than has so far been accorded to it, because it raises once again the issue of anti-dumping legislation as a way of meeting the intention of helping Canadian publications rather than imposing an 80 per cent content rule. Mr. Stevens wrote this:
Content rules are odious in principle and would be a nightmare to administer. A better, simpler way would be to move to an anti-dumping approach. Time and Reader's Digest would not enjoy an unfair competitive advantage if they were forced to pay a realistic price for the news stories and articles they import. National Revenue would come up with a fair price by taking the editorial costs and prorating the cost over circulation in CAnada. Or, it could calculate a price on the basis of what Canadian newspapers pay for foreign wire services, what Canadian television pays for foreign news film, and so on.
I tried to follow the discussion which went on in committee as carefully as I could, but I have never heard any answer from the minister or from a government spokesman explaining why anti-dumping legislation could not be used to secure the end which Bill C-58 envisages. I believe that if our attention were focused on that aspect, as it will be when we come back to the motion for third reading, the issue ought to be raised again.
In addition, thought should be given to a further consideration, that because of the remarkable intervention yesterday by the Minister of National Revenue, the bill should be referred back to committee for reconsideration. The action of the minister yesterday completely distorted the effort of the committee to reach an accommodation which would be founded in law and which would make it possible for Time and Reader's Digest to operate within a formula enabling them to continue to publish in a fair manner and in a manner which, at the same time, was fair to Canadian publications. There was a disposition on the part of members of the committee on both sides to find such a formula but, as is well known, the government refused to consider amendments which the committee was in the process of formulating. This led, of course, to the stage we have now reached, in the course of which amendments have been introduced on a unilateral basis.
I believe the government acted in a wholly improper manner in seeking to protect Reader's Digest following the enormous pressure to which it was subjected in favour of that publication. The government acted in a way which leaves open the question of its sincerity-whether it did seriously intend to find legislation which would improve circumstances in the publishing industry in Canada.
I am saying, finally, that the government has taken a back door approach in bowing to this pressure without coming to the floor of the House of Commons and producing amendments, producing the kind of legislation which would write into law what it seeks to do for Reader's

Digest. If I were the managers of Reader's Digest, I would be worried about what might happen if there were a change of minister, a change in some of the departmental officials who might advise the minister on decisions concerning Reader's Digest a few years down the line. I would be worried, not only about the arbitrary way in which officials of the Department of National Revenue are empowered to make rulings, but also that rulings might be changed, given a change in personnel or a change in government policy.
The government owes us some answers. I say this to the minister: I know he is really trying to help Canadian publishing, and I am on his side. I do not quarrel with the intent of Bill C-58, but I ask him this: What happened between the time he came before the committee shortly before Christmas, when he shot down the process of accommodation to which members on both sides were contributing, when he never even raised the possibility that Reader's Digest could conform to his requirements, and the announcement yesterday by the Minister of National Revenue? Obviously, something happened, because the government changed its mind. I ask the minister to tell us. Let us have the documentation. Let us see the memoranda which have been floating around with figures of 50 per cent, 60 per cent and 80 per cent on them. Let him come clean as to the publishing policy reflected in Bill C-58 so that members of this House and the public at large may have an understanding of what publishing rights are to be protected.

I know how we will get out of it, but I do want hon. members to try to understand the historical genesis of this whole issue. They seem to have come into the issue rather late in the game. Let me take them back a little. It may be rather laborious for them, but perhaps they will learn something. Let me go back again to the one document that we seem to be reasonably agreed upon and which started the process forward. I refer, of course, to the royal commission that studied this matter.
I am not going to read the whole report, but I should like to take a few excerpts from it which seem to me to be germane to the argument in which the House is presently engaged. As all hon. members know, the royal commission studied the state of the Canadian periodical industry and made certain observations and recommendations. One of its interesting observations, under the rubric of the responsibility of the publisher, the royal commission, is as follows:
The right of Canadians to their own media of communication implies that they should not be served with merely a rehash of editorial matter cheaply obtained from abroad for reuse in this country. There can be no excuse for the republication in Canada of periodicals which are not much more than facsimiles of those abroad. Here is something which, whatever may be said of its ethics, does not benefit the public.
That was a general observation from which it drew certain conclusions. The first is as follows:
1.	That a nation's domestic advertising expenditures should be devoted to the support of its own media of communications.
2.	That a nation's communications media must be aware of their responsibilities and that such media should not be used merely for the republication of editorial matter to support an advertising structure.

February 4, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
Thirdly, the commission concluded:
That a Canadian periodical is one published in Canada, owned either by Canadian citizens or, if a corporation, by a company incorporated under the laws of Canada or of one of its provinces, and which is controlled and directed by Canadian citizens and is not a licensee of or otherwise substantially the same as a periodical owned or controlled outside Canada.
Obviously, what has happened historically since then has been an effort, frequently abortive, to try to translate those recommendations into some form of legislative practice. At the time the royal commission was concerned, of course, for the arguments that had been developed by members opposite, and indeed by members of my own caucus, about how the translation of these principles affects the question of freedom of expression. I think hon. members opposite will be generous to enough to concede that it is not simply a concern of their own but of all members of the House. The commission had this to say:
Subject always to paramount national interest, the commission has avoided suggesting measures which limit either the freedom of expression or its corollaries: free flow of information and readership preference.
Some may claim that the statement of an ownership requirement constitutes licensing of the printing press. Such is not the case. The right to own a press and to print and distribute from it whatever is legally permissible, remains unhampered.
The commission's sole purpose is to define those periodicals which by reason of their responsibility to, and function in, the Canadian nation, should be assisted in their access to Canadian advertising expenditures, this in keeping with the principle that the advertisement of domestic goods and services to a domestic consumer should be through a Canadian medium.
The diversion of Canadian advertising from foreign periodicals does not mean regulation of the preparation, content or free flow of their editorial material any more than it means that the reader is denied the periodical of his choice.
Finally, in its emphasis on Canadian advertising support for Canadian media, the Commission's conclusions make neither rules as to what an advertisement may contain nor regulations regarding how much may be spent in periodicals. They simply provide for the spending of money raised from the domestic consumer in support of domestic media.
The commission was concerned lest there might exist in some minds a concept of advertising which would consider this policy a violation of some sort of right or freedom.
That is really where this issue started in a thoughtful and comprehensive way. I think it is fair to say-I am sure there is no dispute in the House about this-that the credentials of the commission were impeccable. Their intent was serious and their efforts were thorough. What we, as members of parliament, have been trying to do-and we are not the first to look at this; our predecessors looked at it, too-is translate those thoughts and those conclusions into some legislative form. The debate we are involved in today, and have been involved in over this past year, really centres around this question.
As I have said several times, Bill C-58 is an attempt to eliminate an anomaly, an exception to the 1965 law which was the first major attempt to translate the recommendations of that royal commission into legislative practice. It attempts to reinstate the full thrust of that 1965 law, and that is all it attempts to do.

Let me reiterate that the government is not seeking in any way to control the freedom of magazine publishers and editors. Nor do we want to impose our will upon the people of Canada and regulate their reading habits. Bill C-58 in no way impinges upon freedom of expression. The bill does not deal with prevention of entry into Canada of information, the curbing of the operation in Canada of any publication, or the imposition of any Canadian content regulations. But it does prevent the dumping of editorial copy. We are not talking about the availability of magazine business in Canada or the choice of reading material by anyone resident in Canada.
I find it difficult to really take seriously some of the arguments I heard in the House last night from members opposite to the effect that this is at play, because the disturbing fact is that 95 per cent of the magazines sold by Canadian newsstands are in fact foreign magazines. Given this fact, it seems to me it is difficult to argue that somehow the free flow of material is being impaired either by the 1965 law or by this amendment.
Bill C-58 is not discriminatory; it seeks to remove an existing discriminatory situation. The present situation whereby both Time and Reader's Digest are exempted from certain stipulations of the Income Tax Act, which apply to the majority of all other consumer and special interest foreign magazines regularly circulating in Canada, is clearly discriminatory. The legislation's intent is to reserve any benefits or concessions associated with the periodical publishing industry for the domestically-owned and controlled segment of that industry. This, historically, has been the practice of all governments vis-a-vis domestic industries.
More particularly, this very approach is consistent with the view held by a considerable number of governments, including one composed of some hon. members now sitting opposite. I should like to touch now, Mr. Speaker, on the ruling made by my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen), that a magazine must be 80 per cent different from a foreign magazine to qualify as Canadian for tax purposes, because obviously this is what is at the root of the hon. member's motion. I should like to interject for a moment to say that I welcome him back from Peterborough, I hope his visit there was successful and that he enjoyed it.

I should like to say that this, perhaps has been the most misunderstood part of the government's attempt to support periodical publishing in this country. First of all, the ruling is not part of Bill C-58. It is an interpretation of a clause in the Income Tax Act which says that a magazine cannot be considered Canadian for tax purposes if it is substantially the same as a magazine published outside the country. It does not apply to newspapers, we are not suggesting it be applied to newspapers, and it has been law since 1965.

No one has argued the necessity for having some sort of definition of Canadian magazines, and no one has questioned the necessity of Canadian ownership as one of the criteria. But we are not dealing with the economics of some manufacturing company; we are dealing with the very nature and quality of our cultural expression. I would like to quote the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) who in 1962 supported in this House the O'Leary royal commission report. At that time he said:
The issues at stake are not essentially of a commercial character, but go into the fabric of our culture.
That is as true now as it was then; in fact, I believe the stakes are even higher now. I think in his very interesting and thoughtful speech the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman) last night, in a more serious way than most of his colleagues, tried to come to grips with this very difficult problem. For those members opposite who did not have the privilege of hearing his speech, I recommend it to them because in it he reached some of the questions which lie at the root of this legislation and the attempts by the government and the opposition parties to deal with the problem of the penetration of the Canadian culture.
If what we are trying to encourage is expression and interplay between Canadians, then we must at the very least permit it to happen. But if what we support is to be Canadian, then we must have a definition. In the case of a magazine-a vehicle for ideas-it is not enough to say that it is owned by a Canadian company. That is where I part company with my very distinguished colleague who I am sure will be speaking later, the hon. member for Vancouv-er-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt). That hon. member has a motion before the House which would restrict it simply to ownership. I say to her, as I will after she speaks, that I do not think that is good enough. She is within her rights to argue for it, and I have the right to argue against it. Who controls what ideas are in it? Surely that is equally important. And if the true control, both financial and editorial, is not in Canadian hands, then I do not think the magazine should be supported by the government. That does not mean it cannot circulate here. It does mean, though, that it should not qualify for special tax privileges which have been instituted to encourage, specifically, Canadian magazines.
When provision in the law was made to exclude magazines which were substantially the same as foreign ones from the benefits, it was done to preclude the possibility of a foreign company setting up a front in Canada, and because the front would be Canadian-owned, benefitting from something for which it did not qualify. In a sense, that is what Time and Reader's Digest have done. Their Canadian companies have full and exclusive rights to use in Canada a vast amount of editorial material which the Canadian companies buy for a fraction of the cost of its production. Yet the true Canadian magazine trying to compete has no access to any similar material. In fact, if a Canadian magazine tried to establish this sort of relationship with a foreign one so that it could compete with Time and Reader's Digest, it would lose the tax privileges it has because it would be substantially the same as a foreign periodical. Time and Digest are not required to meet this part of the law. Bill C-58 will change that.
The questions arise: How different is different? How substantial is substantial? Why 80 per cent? There are
Non-Canadian Publications
those who said that "substantial" should be defined as half; that to be "different" it should be 51 per cent different. Let me deal with that first.

speechtext: Of course.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
That is the position of the hon. member and it is the position of his party. I am looking at it from the point of view of publishing policy and I will develop an argument as to why it should not be 51 per cent or 50 per cent from a publishing point of view. That is my concern. It is not a workable proposition. That decision, of course, obviously is appealable to the courts.
A magazine which was allowed to receive 49 per cent of its material from a foreign source or sources would have a clear competitive advantage over one which tried to produce everything itself. This would be mainly because its costs would be so much lower, for it could buy material which is in a sense used for a fraction of what it costs to produce new or fresh material. The result would be this: in a short time almost all magazines, and certainly all those who had competitors, would be forced to accept this arrangement out of necessity. Magazines producing their own material could not afford to compete with those producing only half of their own material. Gradually, the market would change drastically so that the only magazines left would be those which had an arrangement with a foreign publisher. Because the magazines would be relying so heavily on their foreign suppliers, virtually the entire industry would be dependent on foreign sources.
So when considering the definition of "substantial", the government discarded the concept of "more than half". I think hon. members will have to come to grips with that argument. This is not an argument I alone present; this was the considered position of the Canadian Periodical Publishers' Association. It has been the considered position of other members of this House. It is not good enough simply to say that that conceivably might be an interpretation by the court. What we are determining here, of course, is publishing policy. That may stand or fall in the courts. That is another issue. But it seems to me that when members opposite argue for 50 per cent, they argue that in terms of publishing policy. I think the onus is on them to demonstrate that at 50 per cent, in fact, my scenario would not happen. In fairness to them-and I have the greatest respect for them-I do not think they have done that; I do not think they did it in committee or in this debate. But the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) has yet to speak on his motion and I take it he will address himself specifically to this point which was raised by the Canadian Periodical Publishers' Association, which has been raised by me in committee and, as well, by the hon. member for Sauit Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes).
I would like the hon. member to point out clearly to me and to the House why, if he feels that in fact we should go for 50 per cent, it would not lead to the scenario of a series of split runs in the country. The presumption behind that question is that he himself would not like to see this policy which would lead inevitably to a series of split runs, because he is sufficiently concerned about the state of the industry to object to that. Just to reassure hon. members

that 1 am not simply speaking for myself, a confessed innocent in the field of publishing, I should like to quote a letter which recently appeared in the Globe and Mail, written by someone who is in the field and who had something to say about Bill C-58. The author of the letter is the editor of Chatelaine. It reads:
The content ruling in Bill C-58, however, is being misinterpreted. The suggestion that the content ruling be lowered from 80 per cent to 50 or 60 per cent would completely negate the purpose of the bill. No Canadian magazine could compete with foreign publications that could import almost half of their editorial free-or at nominal cost. It is exactly the same as if we were to tell a Canadian car manufacturer that he must compete with another car manufacturer who gets his engine free.
In fact, if the content ruling were lowered to 50 or 60 per cent "substantially different" it is more than likely that a flood of foreign publications both in consumer magazines and the business press would come into Canada to take advantage of the new ruling. Canadian magazines would be worse off than ever.
I think that fundamentally the question that is at play and that is disputed between the two sides of the House is about 50 per cent versus 80 per cent. What, in fact, would it lead to in terms of the publishing industry? Would it, as I have suggested, lead to a series of split runs? Would it, in fact, lead to a situation where Canadian magazines would cut their losses and go for the cheaper material for half of their content?
Contrary to the claims of some hon. members opposite, the figure of 80 per cent was considered some time ago; in fact, before second reading debate ever started. In February of 1975 the then minister of national revenue said publicly that 80 per cent was a figure which would definitely be acceptable. That was in an interview with the minister which was reported rather widely and to which there was a fairly widespread response, a response somewhat similar to the response we have been getting from the opposition since then. He also said that 60 per cent would be a minimum threshold above which it might be possible to consider magazines, but if they wanted to be sure, then they would strive for 80 per cent. He repeated this in March, but people said it was not clear and I think they have a point.
What was the grey area between 60 per cent and 80 per cent? Because it would be so difficult to administer a grey area fairly, the government made a final decision, announced in October, 1975, by the Minister of National Revenue, that 80 per cent was the amount of difference required to achieve Canadian tax status. This was to ensure that Canadian magazines could have a real chance, and also to ensure that there would be no possibility of the industry being controlled by foreign suppliers of editorial material.
So what happens to Reader's Digest or any magazine which wants to be a digest? Well, if the editors sit down and read the articles available around the world, make their choices, condense their articles and publish them, it is fine. We made that point at some length in the committee. But they cannot buy more than 20 per cent of the already digested and condensed material from someone else who has done it for another magazine while saying they are Canadian.
In the case of Reader's Digest, it means that predigested articles or those orginated by foreign editions of Reader's Digest can only make up 20 per cent of the material in any

given issue. The rest of the work has to be done here with no obligation to a parent company or to foreign editors. Thus, editors and publishers will still remain free to do what they please. For example, they can sell their editorial and financial control to foreign interests and still be able to circulate freely in Canada. I am referring to such magazines as the Economist, Newsweek, Le Nouvel Observateur, and a host of successful foreign magazines. They cannot sell to foreign interests and qualify their advertisers for Canadian tax privileges at the same time. Once again I would say to hon. members that I do not consider this to be censorship. I try to make the case as rationally and dispa-sionately as possible. I think it is common sense.
The hon. member for Edmonton Strathcona has been talking about a back door deal designed to protect Reader's Digest. There has been no deal and there has been no reprieve. I think the Minister of National Revenue made that position abundantly clear last night. What has happened? It should not come as a great surprise to hon. members. Reader's Digest decided to conform with the law, and that was their option.
There are people in this country who support the bill and who view it as a device to get rid of the two magazines, but I have been perfectly candid with the House and with the public that that has never been my intention. My sole intention has been to equalize the impact of the law. If they can conform, surely that is their right. If they decide not to conform, that is equally their right.
What Reader's Digest has decided to do is to conform. That was the announcement that was made, I take it, yesterday or the day before, or whenever it was. I do not think we should underestimate the difficulties ahead of them. I think we are being rather casual about the announcement, and rather machiavellian in searching for motives. The fact is that the task ahead of Reader's Digest, and particularly the publishers of that magazine, is very difficult. To conform, they have to go to 75 per cent ownership, they cannot operate under a licence with their parent company, and they cannot be substantially the same as the U.S. edition. They cannot be, to use the language of the O'Leary report, a pale facsimile.
That is obviously what the announcement was designed to convey to their advertisers, in the first instance, and to the House and the public at large. Having looked at the bill and having, I take it, judged the prospects of getting it through-their judgment on that may be more accurate than mine-they decided to conform with the law. That is something that should not come as a surprise and should not be the subject of prolonged debate. I thought that was always something that both sides of the House viewed as a possibility. The fact that some of us on this side of the House-not all of us-the NDP and two very noble souls in the PC party have argued for the principles of this bill for the past year is something from which we can take some satisfaction in the results so far.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
In respect of motion No. 2, Madam Speaker, the mentality that seems to have dominated the minister, government spokesmen on this bill-I have to differentiate between government spokesmen and those in the government who have had the courage of their convictions, despite some dire consequences that might fall on their heads, and have spoken against this bill-and government supporters of this bill has been one of simply ramming it through the House and the committee. As the 80 per cent clause was not available to us, it was difficult to discuss the aspect of the bill yesterday.
Non-Canadian Publications
After yesterday's announcement concerning Reader's Digest, one was able to detect a new mentality on the part of government supporters. They say, in so many words, that as the opposition has saved Reader's Digest, its objections to this bill should vanish. We oppose the way in which the government was going to force Reader's Digest to cease publication. But we also considered the effect of the legislation on other magazines. Should we not object to the objectionable features of this bill, merely because one magazine was saved by a back door deal? The government is saying, "Well, you have saved Reader's Digest; you have won half the battle. Why not take half a loaf and go home?" The point is that this is not merely a question of saving a magazine, Reader's Digest or any other magazine. The legislation is wrong, immoral and unacceptable. That is why we oppose it.
I sympathize with the aims of the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) in whose name stands motion No. 2. On general principle I oppose content regulations. Probably I can support Canadian ownership provisions. There is nothing wrong with saying that 75 per cent of a magazine should be edited or published in Canada, or that the majority, say three-quarters, of the board of directors should be Canadian. But I object to the principle of any content provision. I object to giving the government, the Department of National Revenue in this instance, the right to determine if content regulations are being obeyed and the standards to be used. I mention standards because the matter is not clear even now.
The minister complains that this debate has been going on for about one year. We have discussed it off and on, that is true, but the issue is more clouded now than it was during the committee discussion. Then, at least, we knew what we were debating. Now it is hard to interpret certain provisions, despite the intervention of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen). On principle, I oppose content regulations. Reader's Digest and Time Canada discussed Canadian content with previous administrations. If my memory serves me correctly, about 30 per cent of Reader's Digest could be considered to be of Canadian content before Bill C-58 was introduced. Time magazine devoted five or six pages per issue to Canadian news. You must concede this, no matter what your views are on the establishment of another Canadian news magazine. Even without the statutory obligation to include material of Canadian content, those two magazines took steps to becoming more Canadian, without any legislative requirement. Evidently, past discussions with those two magazines were fruitful. Perhaps more discussions should have taken place, and perhaps the magazines would have increased their percentage of Canadian content.
To make clear the subject we are debating, the mover of motion No. 2 suggests in his amendment that a magazine should be considered as Canadian, for tax purposes, if more than half the content of any one issue, excluding advertisements, are Canadian, as defined by the Minister of National Revenue. As I said, I do not like content regulations. If this amendment passes, we shall know clearly the content requirement. At least we shall know what we are dealing with, what are the rules of the game. As things now stand, the minister can decide arbitrarily.

February 4, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
Using his discretion, he can introduce any regulations in this field that he wishes.
Passage of the hon. member's motion would mean that the content requirements are spelled out in the statute and we could debate them. Therefore, I hope hon. members will accept the motion, as the content requirements would be clearly defined. Frankly, I feel that the government has done a complete about-face with regard to Reader's Digest. The rules concerning the 80 per cent and 20 per cent relationship have been changed. The figure of 20 per cent now applies, apparently, to matters previously governed by the figure of 80 per cent.
I hope the government whips will allow government supporters freedom to exercise their rights. I hope hon. members opposite will be allowed to vote as they see fit on motion No. 2 or on the motion standing in the name of the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik). Acceptance of either motion would at least narrow the scope of debate and subsequent administrations would know the will of this House. Even I, with all my hang-ups about content rules, am willing to accept the hon. member's amendment so we may know exactly what we are debating. The hon. member for Ontario spoke well last night. His was a constructive, not a critical approach. He did not try to destroy what the minister had achieved. I think an accommodation could be reached with which members of this House could live. I commend the hon. member for his courage and for the clarity with which he spoke yesterday.
Finally, may I say a word about motion No. 3 standing in the name of the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy). I should like to see the scope of his motion expanded to include scientific, medical, trade and agricultural magazines. I live in the naive hope that the government will re-examine its position and allow the motions alluded to, or some of them, to carry in order to make clear what we are debating.
