subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the House for its courtesy. I was in Peterborough, where an unruly student of Trent University classified me as the father of the red Tories. I was able to tell him that although I would be proud to accept that accolade, the title rightly belonged to Benjamin Disraeli, but that I would be glad to account myself as being of that noble line. So much for Peterborough. It is a long drive. My

presence there accounts for my not being here last evening to present this motion.
I want to disabuse the mind of the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) and members of the House about any motives I have in respect of this amendment. It really falls under the conservative part of the Progressive Conservative label. All I was doing was attempting to put in statutory form the judicial interpretation that I have come across of the phrase "not substantially the same". I was being authentically conservative in this regard. Having said that, I hope anybody who feels that way will not now have any difficulty. The hon. member was kind enough to say that although he did not like the content provision in any measure, he saw the point of this amendment.
The minister took the trouble to give us a little of the history of this legislation. If he does not mind, I should like to remind him that at second reading stage I said I thought, in the case of citizenship qualifications, using the phrase rather loosely, it is time that both publications which are really the subject matter of this bill took out their papers at the Canadian court of citizenship. The hon. member who just spoke echoed this feeling. That was not the major preoccupation of our debate either at second reading or at the committee stage.
We were told by representatives of Reader's Digest, and this added to our dilemma, that there was no way they could comply. I must say that I hope I am not now breaking any confidence. On many occasions, when representatives of Reader's Digest came to see me on this issue, I asked as the spokesman for my party why they did not get into the marketplace and get rid of some of their shares. This is a footnote, but I happen to believe that just because one holds shares, control does not necessarily follow. However, that is a semantic or a numbers argument that I do not want to get into.
I am not going to argue with the minister that the 75 per cent figure does not represent citizenship, and I said so on second reading. If that is the government's determination, so be it. If that is an element of citizenship, it is time these publications took up their Canadian citizenship. There was an indication that they were unable to take this step.
We then had the events of the committee hearings and the protestations on behalf of Reader's Digest to the effect that they could not comply with Bill C-58. The pressure was on all of us. I think the minister was generous in alluding to this in respect of his party and the opposition party, all of whom had a genuine interest in trying to see that once the element of citizenship had been fulfilled, these magazines would be able to continue publishing.
I have not been convinced or understood, no matter what people have said in this debate, that a much more simple and better way could not be found to deal with this matter of inexpensive material being used by Time and Reader's Digest. It is curious how this keeps coming up throughout the debate. I am not convinced that a more simple way of dealing with this material could be by handling it under the anti-dumping legislation. I think a review of the history of this legislation and prior legislation will show this to be the fact.
February 4, 1976

Time Canada could well have paid a higher price for the material it uses in its magazine, but this would of course have deprived the coffers of Canada of substantial amounts of money. The minister may not think this is a valid point, or one in respect of which he should comment. It was my understanding that the arrangement was made some years ago that these magazines were getting material at well below cost, but that the coffers of Canada, of the Crown, were benefitting. Certainly the government is justified in changing its opinion as priorities change. Those of us who feel deeply about the continuation of Canadian publications felt that mere tax dollars were not sufficient justification for having material dumped.
Perhaps the minister and others may think I am taking a bit too long to say that the anti-dumping legislation is in place, and that techniques could easily be put in place so that the material Time Canada is using could be dealt with under that legislation. We were told in argument that this would be an interference with the flow of information, We were told that we would have to believe that the 80 per cent rule was not interference, but that the anti-dumping legislation would somehow be translated into interference. Perhaps I was not in Peterborough long enough to understand the subtlety of that argument.
The minister quoted Doris Anderson. She is one of the people in Canada who over the years has been terribly sensitive on the issue of healthy Canadian publications. I want to believe that those who are so anxious about the survival of Canadian periodicals are equally concerned about the monopoly which will ensue if all the publications in Canada are housed under one publisher. That is perhaps not as fundamentally serious to the future of publications in Canada but it is a very major problem for the Secretary of State and his department. Let there be no mistake that I, for one-and many others-will be deeply disappointed if, as a result of all the agony we are going through, all the hearings and debate-and, if I may say so, a fair amount of cries of anguish-all we have done is enhanced or furthered one or two Canadian publications.
At second reading, and I think the minister will not mind hearing this again, I suggested there were a couple of things he could do now to help Canadian periodicals; and that was not six months ago. The first thing I suggested was in respect of the matter of postage. The second thing was that the Crown, as landlord of all these station and airport facilities for the distribution of magazines, could easily make it part of the leases that Canadian magazines have a fair opportunity to purchase. That does not say they will purchase, but an arrangement could be made in the leases to see that Canadian publications have a fair proportion of the exposure, something more than the 5 per cent which is now the case. I have no reason to doubt the minister's figures, but it is a terrible indictment on all of us that 95 per cent of the publications on the newsstands are American.
The minister said, and again I am not going to dispute this because I have no evidence, that the press release which was put in our hands yesterday was not the result of any deal. I am not using the word "deal" in any pejorative sense, nor am I being critical. But, obviously, representatives of Reader's Digest and of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) must have had some discussion and
Non-Canadian Publications
tested a formula-that is perfectly right; there is no reason why they should not-otherwise Reader's Digest would not have been able to make the statement it did.
But let us say the hon. member for Fundy-Royal believed all the evidence given by periodicals and ebelieved the minister's own evidence before the standing committee. The minister surely did not say that the Digest could not survive, but the Canadian periodical industry certainly said that unless legislation based on the 80 per cent formula was part and parcel of government policy, Reader's Digest and Time would continue. Now we find that despite all this, Reader's Digest finds it can continue. The minister would surely agree that this places us in a peculiar position. One wonders whether all the discussion which has taken place, all the evidence and all the hearings were not really a waste of time. I do not think the minister should be surprised if we are taking a day or two to discuss this new situation. Presumably, this is what was in the mind of the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) when he suggested the committee should have another crack at hearing about the arrangement.
With reference to my complimentary remarks about Doris Anderson, I would be very interested to see-I do not suppose the mails have brought this yet, but perhaps the telegrams have started to come-what Mrs. Anderson thinks of the arrangement Reader's Digest has made with the Department of National Revenue. Will she write another letter to the Globe and Mail saying, "fine, the Canadian Periodicals' Association is happy to welcome a new citizen," a new member, presumably, of the association. Let us be fair about this. Has the mail begun to pile up? Has the minister received any telegrams?
I have another point to make. It is quite a serious one and I hope that before the debate on motion No. 2 is concluded the minister or one of the members opposite speaking for him can answer a rather important question. What arrangements concerning a time-frame have been made between the Department of National Revenue and the Canadian edition of Reader's Digest so that the Digest can get itself into the new form which will meet the test of the content rule? Will there be an interim period during which the Digest does not qualify and is, therefore, beyond the law if this law passes in the foreseeable future? Or will Reader's Digest Canada be allowed a transitional period during which it can come aboard, so to speak, and make the arrangements which are necessary?
As I understand the press release, the attributes of citizenship, for example, the selling of 45 per cent of the shares to make up 75 per cent, as is necessary under this bill, could not be accomplished immediately Reader's Digest could not be expected to do this in the month of February, and presumably it would take several months for Reader's Digest Canada to put itself into the position of being acceptable within the content rule and other parts of section 19 of the Income Tax Act. The minister apologized; he has left the chamber. The Minister of National Revenue is not in the House. But I would hope that before the debate on my amendment, No. 2, is concluded somebody on behalf of the government will satisfy the House in this regard because a matter of fairness is involved.

February 4, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
No matter how vigorously the government is opposed, citizens in a democratic state expect there should be fairness shown to all, so the House is entitled to know what time-frame has been allowed to Reader's Digest to come on board as far as content, ownership and such matters are concerned. If that question could be answered we would soon be ready, I presume, to vote on my amendment. What I have attempted to say-and I have tried to do this without a series of elegantly drafted notes-is this: I want to know the time-frame for Reader's Digest because it is my expectation that a fair and small "1" liberal government will be granting the same transitional period to every publication requiring time to meet the test of section 19. If I could be sure that the same transitional arrangement is to be allowed others in order to join this happy group of new Canadian publications, we would be able to proceed quite rapidly.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my first temptation is to take the compliments of the minister and run. I hope he will feel the same way after my contribution, on a point of principle, today. At any rate, I thank him for his generous remarks. I wonder what his reaction was when he heard that Reader's Digest would, indeed, comply. He indicated today that he received the news with pleasure, but I wonder whether deep down it was really so and whether we have really reached the end of this question.
The minister began by saying he was not a professional journalist or publisher, and that in those circumstances he had to take the advice of people who were. I will begin by mentioning two people who are professional journalists- Geoffrey Stevens and Charles Lynch, two of our most respected reporters. What do those professional writers tell us? I am sure the minister knows that these people do not support the bill. They decline to do so on important questions of principle. I wondered how the minister would respond to the Reader's Digest announcement and I think perhaps Geoffrey Stevens had it right when he said this:
Beyond that, there is the question of what happens if Time somehow manages to survive and continues to attract Canadian advertising. A prediction: the government, having taken one highly discriminatory step with its 80 per cent content rule, would be hard pressed to resist taking another even more discriminatory action to get rid of the magazine.
I suspect that might well be so, and it concerns me. It concerns me that the principal steps, many of them very good steps that I support, might be taken to excess and be one more step down the road to what Charles Lynch says is manipulation of content. That is the angle that concerns me. He said:
Indeed, news is being manipulated in many countries but Canada is not one of them. For us to join the list would be very bad business.
I share that concern, Mr. Speaker, and in talking to it, if I use overstatement or political licence excessively, I apologize. But I do so only to make this point of principle. When I was in India only a few months ago, the Speaker of one of the state legislatures in that country stoutly defended Mrs. Gandhi's emergency measures and her admonishments of an irresponsible press. He reassured me that I need have no concern regarding democracy and freedom of the press in India because Mrs. Ghandi was a true demo-

crat and these stern, non-legislated controls would soon be lifted. Four months later the same Speaker saw his own legislature permanently dissolved by the central government, and legislation for the complete censorship of the press passed and enacted, all within the framework of a democratic constitution by a leader espousing and extolling democracy as the justification for her actions.
I am not suggesting that we are anywhere near this kind of situation in Canada, but even the smallest move in this direction of interference should be observed, enunciated and put to rest; because a democratic principle must always take precedence over an expedient one, no matter how important an issue the expediency might resolve. I suggest that tampering with content is tampering with the democratic principle in order to accomplish an expedient end. The expedient end I might even agree with, but even if I were to agree with it I could not compromise my principles and I do not think the minister could either.
I would agree that those who protest the content regulation are using considerable political licence when they call the content move outright censorship. However, if it is not outright censorship it is a form of restriction which inhibits and suppresses, a position perilously close to censorship. The initial steps toward censorship in any democratic state are usually orchestrated slowly and subtly. In India, in November, no specific legislation existed to exercise this power, but the press was warned and knew that their editorial and story line must be "substantially the same as" that of the government and more than "80 per cent substantially different" from that of the previously so-called irresponsible press. This unlegislated, yet insidious moral suasion in India largely accomplished its aim, and after several months of "80 per cent substantially the same" government line a final legislative death-blow to the press was easily accomplished, the press having fallen victim to its own unwilling axe.
I ask the minister to examine carefully his own use of insidious moral suasion, and suggest that this legislation, through its content rule, might be the exercise of the sort of power I have referred to. I ask the minister, would Time magazine dare print today an anti-government story in recent editions, or would such moral suasion encourage them to feature the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on the front of their magazine and suddenly find its Canadian section important enough to feature lavish, full colour photo coverage of the Prime Minister's travels? Or would it be possible that we might see CTV news suddenly downplaying the role of opposition members and promoting government members and programs? I would say probably not, because they know that earlier a prominent proCanadian member said that there is not, and could not be, any question of interference with the press in so far as the dissemination of news and opinion is concerned. "I know that no Liberal government would ever think of doing so"-so said the famous Walter Gordon in 1965. It was to his credit, as a nationalist, that he said we must not tamper with the press and its content in any way. Yet that is what we are doing today. I am sure he would share my concern and the concern of other members in this regard.
Certainly the minister should be watching closely that vested interest remains the dominating consideration in the passage of this legislation, rather than the control of
February 4, 1976

content for some lofty nationalistic, Canadian objective. Even by touching the issue of any form of content legislation or regulation the government is setting itself on a dangerous course. I would urge it to reconsider.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) says it is important to understand that "not substantially the same" does not refer to subject matter. Well, what does it refer to? The colour of the ink? It seems to me that "content" and "subject matter" are substantially the same type of synonym. The amendment is a very difficult compromise and I shall vote for it with great reluctance. While I would vote for the amendment with great reluctance, favouring the 60 per cent rule, I would vote against the legislation if any concept of content control is to be found in the legislation, on the basis of the infringement of a basic democratic principle. I ask the minister to consider that carefully.
In Canada we are a long way from India but only a short step away from legislating a highly dangerous precedent on the route to content control. When the minister said that we want a situation where there is no interference in the freedom of Canadians to read Time and Reader's Digest, I am sure he would add "or any material of their interest". But if interference does result in the material not being available, obviously we defeat our purpose. Does the minister have evidence from Time Canada that the magazine will be available to read subsequent to the passage of this legislation? Unfortunately, negotiations seem to be going on outside the House and committee and we must read the results in the press. Having read the results and found that Reader's Digest can live with the legislation, let me ask the minister whether similar negotiations are going on with Time. Will Time actually survive, as Reader's Digest will, in his opinion? If it will not survive, then he is indeed infringing the rights of Canadians to read material of their choice.
I am pleased that the minister sees this bill as part of an attempt to define Canadianism. I am also pleased that we are proceeding to a further type of definition of what is Canadian and what is a Canadian magazine. Were he to move toward ownership, publishing control, and so forth, I think all Canadians would be pleased. But he is going further when he tampers with content. I feel confident that the minister, because of his integrity, does not like this content provision any more than the rest of us in this House. I am sure he shares the principle of non-intervention and that he would like to find some other way.
I am not suggesting the other way that he might find, because I think his search will be long and hard. However, I ask that he not give way to expediency now, that he take out the content section of this bill and immediately assign to a committee terms of reference to the effect that it should find a way other than content.
Let us listen, perhaps, to some of the suggestions of the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather), but above all let us take the great principles that have been advanced in this bill and keep them, and let us not tarnish the bill with an attack on content, on whether it is censorship or whether it inhibits. Let us take this out and then go ahead and bring the bill into play in the interest of Canadi-
Non-Canadian Publications
an culture, Canadianism and the principles that were enunciated and supported earlier at second reading.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I enter the debate at this report stage with some sense of urgency as we discuss this regressive and depressive step which has been resisted by many thinking writers in Canada whose professional qualities, I think, should certainly appeal to the minister and whose words should be read very carefully by him and the officials of his department.
The bill was fought out in the committee in a way that not many bills are. The minutes will show this. They will also show that on several occasions it went beyond comedy and into farce. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Miss Holt), has already alluded to some of the difficulties presented to some hon. members in attempting to be heard during the committee study. One has great difficulty in knowing what most of the points of the committee study were, but I think a point of some kind was raised when the minister fled the meeting as the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway was about to speak. She was only able to speak because of the gracious motion of the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) that she be heard.
We again saw some rather strange developments in the history and transition of the committee stage during the study of Bill C-58. Any of the authorities on the Canadian parliamentary system who hail the committee system as being the one thing that would save this institution, or that would greatly assist this institution in its deliberations, should read the minutes of the committee as it discussed Bill C-58.
I think it is very important that the rules be grounded in law and that we should consider the point raised by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), that we must indeed pay most careful attention to this question. It is very easy to slip away from "substantially different" into saying 80 per cent, 50 per cent or 20 per cent Canadian content. Again, I think a reading of the minutes of the committee will show that that slip was made frequently both by members and by witnesses. One would suspect, still, that the intent of the bill and the intent of the formula submitted by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) is really obscured by the term "substantially different" and there will be a gradual transition by which it will be interpreted as Canadian content with all that that implies.
I take no pleasure in noting that Reader's Digest has made some kind of a deal with the government. I expect it was easier for the Reader's Digest to do so partly because, to its credit, it has gone a long way in Canadianizing its operation and making its publication a forum for Canadian writers, and also because of the very nature of the digest aspect of the publication. A reading, again, of the minutes of the committee when certain questions were asked about what would constitute "substantially different" qualifications would lead one to suspect that a possible way around this provision would have to do with the timing of the publication, and whether this might be the road to take or a loophole in the legislation that has been found.
Again, I think the call of the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) is worth considering, because it

February 4, 1976
Non-Canadian Publications
would be helpful to the committee and certainly to the House in these final stages of debate on the bill if we were to know just what the arrangements are in respect of Reader's Digest. In all of this, I think we are still missing the basic reason for the situation to which the minister alluded in his remarks when he pointed out that 95 per cent of the publications read in Canada come from outside the country. The hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fair-weather) picked that up and said it was to odr shame. On one level, that is true. Certainly, on another level it is not, because I do not think the problem all along really has been one of content. It has been one of tone, style and appeal to basic values which I believe are still basic to the Canadian way of life.
The problem for any journal or any publication in Canada is to gain and to hold readership. That is the problem, because advertising depends on readership and not on tax concessions, in the last analysis. It depends on the power of the publication to deliver an audience to the advertisers. We tend to lose track of that over and over again, but that is the basic question. We have the problem in respect of Canadian publications which blithely set about losing their readership and then cry for government intervention in order to save them from bankruptcy. When we had the debate on second reading, I referred to Saturday Night. It, coincidentally, had been restructured at the precise time of the debate.
I went through the first of the resurrected issues of Saturday Night with a good deal of pleasure. I made reference to the timing and said that they were on the right track. I was not being entirely facetious when I complimented them for having printed a poem which rhymed. This created a bit of a response from the editorial office of Saturday Night, because they said they never print poems which rhyme. They said that the hon. member for Okana-gan-Kootenay was so illiterate that he failed to notice this. However, someone spotted the fact that it rhymed once. The author of the poem immediately wrote to Saturday Night that her poem contained ten rhymes which were missed because many of them were internal to the structure of the poem and were not strictly at the end of the line. The editor said he found only one after a close, textural study of the work.
Again, the question here is one of editorial policy and editorial judgment. It is not really a question of censorship at all, but of deals that are made between authors and publishers. They are made by editors who decide on the tone of the publication, and through that the authors learn what their chances are in the market. It is with enormous disappointment that I read recently the October, 1975, issue of Saturday Night. I could read it only recently, Madam Speaker, because of the most unhappy mail strike which went on and on. Believe me, the worst aspects of the mail strike were not simply that I could not read Saturday Night until just a week or two ago; there were far worse aspects to it. In all of the debate about content, readership, and so on, we tend to overlook such basic and fundamental questions as postal rates, which play such an important part in the demise of far too many Canadian publications. When one looks through this issue, one can see what the problem is in terms of Canadian content. The content is as

Canadian as can be and it is substantially different because nobody else will print much of it.
At the beginning we find the editor, Mr. Fulford, making his comments in a long article on John Herbert's play "Fortune and Men's Eyes", a play which deals with the sordidness of prison life and deviations, homosexuality in particular. It is not everybody's cup of tea. Then he has a second article about developments in the school system in Ontario, and he takes a knock at oversimplification in a typical school text. The motions refer to the whole matter of the 50 per cent "substantially different". I feel, with due deference, that what I am saying is germane to this topic because surely we would not have Bill C-58 if the kind of problems I am suggesting here did not arise. There has been a lapse of time since the second reading debate. The bill has gone through the committee and has been pushed forward willy-nilly by the government. There has been no reason for any Canadian publication which has looked to a boom in its readership once Bill C-58 has been passed, to be pessimistic, because I think they saw that the government was determined to ram Bill C-58 through second reading, through the committee, through the report stage and through third reading. So, with deference, I feel that what I am saying is germane to the topic because of the lapse of time between second reading and the changes that have occurred with regard to this publication.
I will attempt to be brief. There is an article by Singer and Rodgers on mercury, the hidden poison in the northern rivers. This is a sad story which shows little knowledge of either Canadian native Indians or of the people of Japan. There is also an article about two artists, the Bobaks. I have nothing but praise for it. I own a Bobak print myself. To quote Bobak: "Anglo-Saxons hate to get too personal, too intimate". This is putting a finger on what has been one of the problems in Canadian journalism. Doug Fetherl-ing has an article entitled "Portrait of a Canadian actress waiting for something to happen", who is quoted as saying, "Canada is the country that taught me to be paranoid". I checked the suggestion, the individual responsibility. The idea that a nation does things to individuals within it is too simple altogether.
George Woodcock writes on the perils of freedom in India. This has already been alluded to by a previous speaker, so again I am sure it is very germane to the topic we are discussing. To quote again: "Mrs. Gandhi set in motion the same mechanism of a responsible tyranny which the British used to combat". Yet surely since the trial of Warren Hastings no British rule in Canada could be described as irresponsible because he was called to the bar of justice in a famous trial. Martin Knelman writes on the ghost of "Seven Days" which still mocks the CBC. He refers to the parliamentary committee which studied that program, but he shows no evidence of having read the

minutes of the committee which investigated that particular matter.
There is an excerpt from Robertson Davies' "World of Wonders", and again there is nothing but praise for the totality of Robertson Davies' three part trilogy which may yet be the great Canadian novel, or be considered as such; but it deals with a sordid episode of sexual deviation. Anne Hardy is tough on Alberta. She writes on dining and says that one cannot expect to find good restaurants in English Canada. So much for the third force on the prairies. I am sure that when this issue is read, various readers will decide that that is the last issue of Saturday Night for them. Worst of all, there is an article by Mordecai Richler, reviewing The Swastika and the Maple Leaf, in which he renews the suggestion that a governor general of this country, Lord Tweedsmuir, better known as John Buchan, the novelist, was anti-Semitic. I would rather go to the gas chamber than read the quote that is attributed to him. The author put words in the mouth of a character in chapter one of his book "The Thirty-Nine Steps", which was written in 1915, and Richler uses those words to prove that John Buchan was anti-Semitic.

Madam Speaker, earlier today, on the advice of Mr. Speaker, I raised a question on a point of order relating to the deduction of advertising expenses for income tax purposes. At that time the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) stated that he thought the answer to the question was yes. I asked for an unequivocal yes because I think it is of utmost importance to producers of Canadian livestock to know exactly where they stand as they advertise in these publications, because of the fact that they will not know until a year from this April whether their expenses will be legitimate or not.
It seems to me that it would be logical to put legislation in place for the benefit of the industry so that those people will know they will be protected. We can accomplish this by passing just a subamendment to the amendment we are discussing at the present time, motion No. 3. At the conclu-
Non-Canadian Publications
sion of my speech to-day I propose to move that subamendment.
My reason for moving this subamendment is that the Department of National Revenue was not in a position to give an unequivocal yes to the question I asked. The question is, can the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cullen) state unequivocally that Canadian producers of purebred and exotic livestock will be permitted to deduct costs of advertising in the United States as legitimate expenses for income tax purposes in Canada? The question is that the producer may be called upon to prove that his is a legitimate expense, and he must prove it under clause 1 where it says:
19. (1) In computing income, no deduction shall be made in respect of an otherwise deductible outlay or expense of a taxpayer for advertising space in an issue of a non-Canadian newspaper or periodical dated after December 31, 1975, for an advertisement directed primarily to a market in Canada.
The key words there are "advertisement directed primarily." It could well be that there is not another magazine, periodical or newspaper which would sufficiently advertise the product which the producer has to offer, whether it be young animals or older animals, and it could well be that the producer might go to a United States periodical which is circulated in Canada. He might sell a small percentage, 10 per cent or 15 per cent-it does not really matter; we do not need to discuss figures-in the United States, but the major portion of his sales would be made in Canada. This bill says "advertisement directed." It could well be that while this periodical covers a greater part of the North American continent, this particular advertisement could be directed to people in Canada because of the geographical location of the product which is for sale and also of the purchaser.
This bill is open to interpretation. This is the problem I have had with this legislation right from the start. The Minister of National Revenue, when he spoke about "not substantially the same", said yesterday that it would take time to bring in a ways and means motion to set this up by statute so that we would then know what we are talking about. There could be a great deal of difference between what the Minister of National Revenue, the Secretary of State and I think "not substantially the same" means. It is because of this individual interpretation that we are having problems with this legislation. This is of fundamental importance and individual interpretation is not necessary because it could be spelled out by legislation, and that is what is wrong here. When we are dealing with something of such magnitude, the government is doing a disservice by bringing in legislation to be administered by interpretation rather than by statute.
Yesterday the minister also used the phrase "continuing arrangement." Goodness me, "continuing arrangement" can mean a great deal to a great many people. It might even mean the consummation of marriage between two people. It could mean many things. I do not think the government is performing a useful function when it asks us to accept such vague terms. It boils down to the fact that this is just one man's interpretation, and this is causing a great deal of trouble.
I could go on in this debate, and I hope I will have the opportunity to go into further detail, but at this time I should like to move my subamendment so that Mr. Speaker

will have the opportunity of looking at it and of seeing whether it is acceptable in his judgment. If it is not acceptable, I still should like to have the opportunity of presenting my argument to the House so that it may be fully considered because of its very great importance. I have other things to say on this matter, but because it is almost six o'clock perhaps I can have that privilege at another time.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain):
That the amendment be amended by deleting the words "scientific or medical subjects" and by substituting therefor the words "scientific, agricultural of medical subjects."
Madam Speaker, may I have the privilege of debating this at another time, if you see fit to accept this subamendment? May I call it six o'clock?
